newsitem.title: USA: Dataquest sees booming worldwide chip card market.
newsitem.headline: Dataquest sees booming worldwide chip card market.

text.p: The worldwide market for chip cards is expected to explode as consumers try to simplify their banking and shopping needs with the use of just one card, Dataquest said Tuesday.

Shipments of the plastic cards -- which can function as small change, debit and credit cards all rolled in one -- is expected to surge from 774 million units in 1996 to 3.4 billion units by 2001, the San Jose, Calif.-based market research firm said.
The top-selling region for chip cards is Europe, which accounted for 90 percent of chip-card sales in 1995. Dataquest analysts expect other regions to offer more of these cards this year.

Chip cards, embedded with integrated circuits with simple memory, are most commonly used as prepaid telephone cards in Europe. Phone cards in the United States typically use older technology that requires a magnetic stripe or a personal identification number.

About 471 million memory cards were sold worldwide in 1995, Dataquest said. But the fastest-growing area is in smart cards, which reached 84 million units in 1995 and is forecast to reach 1.2 billion units in 2001, Dataquest said.

Smart cards have more advanced computer chips that can record data about a user's bank account or health, and can be used as an "electronic purse" to buy small items, as well as a credit or debit card. Smart cards are being tested by financial institutions and were used at the Olympic Games in Atlanta.

"Although some standards issues, infrastructure issues, and software issues remain to be resolved, chip cards hold the promise of being one of the world's highest-volume markets for semiconductors," said Jonathan Cassell, analyst in Dataquest.
"Chip cards insert semiconductor technologies into areas where they have never been before, providing a new frontier of growth for integrated circuit makers."
Dataquest is a unit of Gartner Group.
